title: Caleb Williams has shown hints of greatness. How can he make his next big leap? The Bears quarterback remains under an intense spotlight with much of the football world curious to see where his career path is headed. Dan Wiederer and Kevin Fishbain
summary:

full_text:
As he looks to improve in his second season in the Ben Johnson offense, Bears quarterback Caleb Williams says he's “110 percent in” on whatever his coach says. Geoff Stellfox / Getty Images
Caleb Williams is in good hands. The Chicago Bears quarterback made that clear himself throughout this offseason, expressing his growing belief in Ben Johnson as the overseer of his development and the leader of a team that continues to raise its bar.
“Coaching matters,” Williams said in April, then later praising Johnson for “his information, his knowledge, his wisdom.”
“It goes a long way for me,” Williams added. “I’m 110 percent in on whatever he says.”
Best of all, Williams and Johnson have connected on a deeper level with both men understanding their shared ambition will only result in grand accomplishments if they remain united in their dedication to improvement.
“There’s so much to unlock,” Williams said after the Bears’ final practice of the spring. “There’s so much to get better at. There’s so much ball left for me and us.”
After winning the NFC North last season, then notching the franchise’s first playoff victory in a decade and a half, Williams and the Bears have moved well past the feel-good celebration of 2025 and are focused on sustaining their success.
Williams will check into training camp this weekend preparing for Wednesday’s first full-team practice in Lake Forest, Ill., with full understanding of the Bears’ opportunity this season — and a firm grasp on what it will take for both him and the team to get where they want to go.
To set the stage for the six-week on-ramp that will take the Bears toward the regular season, The Athletic ’s Dan Wiederer and Kevin Fishbain discuss what’s ahead for Williams during camp and how his growth will be shaped in 2026.
Dan Wiederer: The one thing I think everybody must understand is the Caleb conversation is only growing louder and more opinionated. For us to continue bringing perspective and nuance into the ring, it will be important to emphasize the developmental targets being set by the coaches at Halas Hall this season. More on those here shortly.
But even before camp begins, the intrigue surrounding Williams’ present and future continues growing and the range of assessments remains vast. At the beginning of this month, three-time Super Bowl champion and current NFL analyst Mark Schlererth made waves with his emphatic opinion that Williams is “not a good quarterback.” (Schlereth’s follow-up explanations offered more layers to an initial take that seemed extreme.)
A few weeks later, ESPN — after polling more than 70 league executives, coaches and scouts — stamped Williams as the NFL’s No. 10 quarterback heading into 2026. Just like that, we had multiple high-profile evaluations that featured either harsh criticism or promising praise.
As we await Mike Sando’s always enlightening “QB Tiers” exercise for The Athletic , where’s your head at with Chicago’s QB1 as we head for training camp? Are you comfortable approving a top-10 ranking for Williams? And — pardon the pun — how much of a “Stink” do you think Schlereth’s comments should have caused?
Kevin Fishbain: This is somewhat unfamiliar territory for us in Chicago. I don’t know how long that ESPN poll has been a summer staple, but I don’t recall any former Bears quarterbacks making that list — or even sniffing it. That speaks to how much Williams’ dazzling sophomore season resonated with the league’s decision-makers and evaluators.
To piggyback on your nuance point, how many quarterbacks in the league — right now — would you rather have the ball in their hands in the final minute of a close game than Williams? He has proved over and over again his ability to make magic happen.
However, Williams wasn’t perfect at the end of games. And there are several reasons the Bears needed him to put on that Superman cape — they had dug themselves a hole, and one of those reasons was Williams’ own inconsistencies early in games. Breaking down his stats as a whole, he might appear to be an average starting quarterback. Viewing it through the lens of what he’s capable of — and what he accomplished in the wins over the Packers and Bengals, among others — reflects a quarterback who can give defensive coordinators nightmares.
I get why someone like Schlereth is not really moved by Williams’ performance when focusing on his completion percentage or the games in which the offense sputtered early. I also was in the building to see Williams take apart the 49ers defense on national television and then perform brilliantly against the Packers with the world watching and the game on the line. Twice. That was top-10 material. I guess I didn’t really answer the question, which is why that position is so tricky.
Wiederer: My unwavering take is that summer lists are always less meaningful than winter lists. They’re often projections more than evaluations. So some of these July conversations don’t really move the needle for me as much as they might for others. Yet I feel certain Williams is in the driveway if not knocking on the door of that top-10 category. (Which, to your point, is an unfamiliar place to be in Chicago.)
That said, consistency is the name of the game. And significant improvement is a must but not a given for the Bears’ QB1 in 2026. To continue his ascent, Williams must remain locked in with Johnson, who is pushing his young quarterback to improve his completion percentage and accuracy; become much more dialed in with the system; and understand efficiency and exactness while still leaning into his creative and dynamic playmaking gifts.
“I’m Caleb Williams’ No. 1 believer,” Johnson said as last season concluded. And that feeling seems to be mutual.
Johnson loved the growth Williams showed in 2025 with his operation command and pocket presence. He expects a big jump in the entire offense’s extended play production this year. And Johnson has also promised to do a better job creating plays where Williams can more regularly feast with opportunities to hit his open primary receiver.
Training camp should offer a fun glimpse into Williams’ direction. With that in mind, where will you have your lens once these practices get rolling?
Fishbain: The ever-elusive consistency. It’s funny to think the Bears finally have someone gifted enough to win a playoff game, but what I’m most interested in watching isn’t much different than what I wrote about Jay Cutler or Mitch Trubisky or Justin Fields heading into camp — consistently sustaining drives.
It can be easy to forget after the success of last season what a mess last summer’s camp was at times for the offense. That got sorted out come Week 3, and the offense did things we haven’t seen in Chicago in a long time. How will that look in camp this summer?
We know defensive coordinator Dennis Allen will try to make things difficult, but can Williams keep the offense on the field drive after drive? Can the unit avoid pre-snap penalties?
I’m intrigued, too, to watch the Williams-Colston Loveland and Williams-Luther Burden connections continue to grow. There’s no ceiling on those two pass catchers and they were go-to, big-play targets for Williams down the stretch. How much of that potential can we see in camp?
What will be on your Caleb camp checklist?
Wiederer: You know how this works. The jaw-dropping plays — and there will be a handful every week — will go viral. They will give social media users an adrenaline rush and push Bears fans to let their imaginations run wild with what may be possible for this quarterback and this team. But what will be celebrated internally at Halas Hall will be Williams’ day-after-day steadiness. His ability to operate. His ability to master the playbook. His ability to understand what he’s seeing from a defense and respond properly. His ability to deliver routine passes with pinpoint precision.
Those are things that will unlock a new level for Williams and this offense.
At this point, the entire football world…

title: The Colts' 10 most indispensable players: Who can Indy least afford to lose? We picked five players on offense and five on defense who would derail the Colts' season if lost for a significant time. James Boyd

She witnessed it firsthand last year when the Colts starte
full_text:
Running back Jonathan Taylor, left, quarterback Daniel Jones, center, and guard Quenton Nelson, right, are all critical to the Colts' success in 2026. Luke Hales / Getty Images
Every NFL team has players it can’t afford to lose. Injuries and other absences are always a factor in a franchise’s direction, and Indianapolis Colts owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon is no stranger to how quickly a team can collapse when key players start missing games. She witnessed it firsthand last year when the Colts started 8-2 and ended 8-9. Irsay-Gordon, however, likened the Colts’ unraveling to pressing pause on a movie. She claimed the conclusion to the 2025 campaign wasn’t the real ending, noting the Colts’ wide array of injuries, most notably to quarterback Daniel Jones.
This year, Irsay-Gordon is hopeful that with better health and a revamped roster, this version of the Colts can deliver an Oscar-worthy finish by finally ending their five-year playoff drought. Some may think her faith is admirable. Others may view it as naïve. Either way, how far the Colts go will likely be determined by the performance of their most indispensable players. Who are they? Let’s take a look at the top 10 players the Colts cannot afford to lose in 2026.
It’s obvious, but there’s no other place to start than with the starting quarterback. The Colts stamped Jones as the face of their franchise by rewarding him this offseason with a two-year, $88 million contract that included $50 million guaranteed at signing. Last year, he was playing at a Pro Bowl-level before fracturing his left fibula, which he played through, and then suffering a season-ending torn right Achilles. Questions about Jones’ mobility and durability are valid, and if he’s unable to regain his pre-injury form — or worse, if he suffers another major injury — the Colts may as well kiss their playoff hopes goodbye. Riley Leonard and Anthony Richardson Sr., who are competing for the backup job, are fine reserve options if Jones misses a few games, but they’re too volatile to rely on for an extended period of time.
Taylor is so vital to the Colts’ success this year that there’s a compelling argument for him to hold-in for a new contract before he steps foot on the field again. The three-time Pro Bowler is coming off his second straight season of at least 1,400 rushing yards, and he totaled a league-high 20 touchdowns in 2025. Indianapolis hardly has any reliable depth behind Taylor, with rookie seventh-round pick Seth McGowan and 2025 fifth-round pick DJ Giddens jockeying for the backup role. Giddens totaled just 96 rushing yards in nine games last season. Make no mistake, if Taylor misses time, the Colts’ running game will be in big trouble.
Raimann inked a four-year, $100 million contract extension last year that solidified him as the Colts’ left tackle of the future. Playing at a high level is even more critical this year considering Jones is returning from an Achilles injury. Indianapolis can’t afford for Jones to constantly be under duress from his blindside, so Raimann must be a pillar of consistent protection, or else Indy’s whole offense will crumble.
Pierce takes over as the Colts’ undisputed No. 1 receiver after the team retained him on a four-year, $114 million deal and subsequently traded veteran Michael Pittman Jr. to the Pittsburgh Steelers. Pittman led the Colts in receptions in four of the past five seasons. Pierce will see an increased target share in Pittman’s absence, but what makes him special is his ability to stretch the field. The 26-year-old, who is currently rehabbing from left ankle surgery , has led the league in yards per reception in each of the past two seasons, and his ability to attack the deep part of the field cannot be replicated by anyone else on the roster if he goes down.
Nelson is on a Hall of Fame trajectory, evidenced by the eight straight Pro Bowl nods he’s earned to start his career. The only other offensive lineman in NFL history to do that: Cleveland Browns legend Joe Thomas. Similar to Raimann, Nelson’s presence is even more important this year when noting that Jones will try to complete his first full season since 2022, which, fittingly, is when he led the New York Giants to the playoffs for the first time in six years. The Colts, obviously, are hoping to replicate that success.
Latu takes the top spot on defense for two reasons: First, he plays arguably the most important position, and second, the Colts have no other proven difference-makers at defensive end on their roster. Because of that, they need Latu, a 2024 first-round pick and the first defensive player drafted that year, to have a breakout season. He played well last year, tallying three interceptions, 12 tackles for loss and 8.5 sacks. This year, he must crack double digits in the sack department, something a Colts player hasn’t done since Justin Houston recorded 11 sacks in 2019. If Latu isn’t a game-changer up front, Indy’s defense will fall apart at the point of attack.
Gardner is entering his first full season with the Colts after being acquired in a blockbuster trade deadline deal last year with the New York Jets. Of course, Gardner’s performance will garner plenty of attention since Indy surrendered two first-round picks to get him. He’s supposed to be the unquestioned top dog in the cornerback room, and he’ll have plenty of chances to prove it amid a schedule that features standout wide receivers Nico Collins, Justin Jefferson, CeeDee Lamb, DeVonta Smith and Ja’Marr Chase, among others. It’ll be Gardner’s job to help shut them down while elevating the Colts’ secondary.
Buckner has been noncommittal this offseason about when he will return from the neck surgery he underwent at the end of last season. That’s troubling for a Colts defense that needs Buckner to return to his All-Pro form. If he isn’t that player, or close to it, that means he won’t command the double-teams that are critical to creating one-on-one opportunities for defensive linemates. Sure, defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo is known for being creative with his schemes and generating pressure, but no amount of ingenuity can replace what Buckner brings to the table when he’s fully healthy.
Stewart has long been one of the unsung heroes of the Colts’ defense. The jovial big man, who is often cracking jokes in the locker room, is a menace on the field and still one of the best run stoppers in the NFL. His ability to clog the middle and stuff runs grants the rest of the defensive line the opportunity to get after the quarterback when foes are forced into passing situations. A healthy and productive Stewart will also go a long way in helping Indy’s new starting linebacker tandem behind him, which will most likely be headlined by rookie second-round pick CJ Allen.
Coachable, high-IQ defender who’s often a step ahead of his teammates; a likely starter.
Bynum, who inked a four-year, $60 million deal to join the Colts last year, delivered in his first season in Indy. He registered a career-high four interceptions and eight passes defensed in 2025. Bynum may get overlooked when discussing Indy’s defense since his teammates, Latu and Gardner, play more premium positions. But with Indy poised to potentially start rookie third-round pick A.J. Haulcy at strong safety, Bynum’s experience should help shore up Indy’s last line of defense. Bynum is also the only safety on the Colts’ roster who’s been a full-time starter in the past two years.

Quarterback Patrick Mahomes has made remark
full_text:
All eyes will be on quarterback Patrick Mahomes in training camp as he returns from a season-ending knee injury. Jamie Squire / Getty Images
Kansas City Chiefs training camp gets its unofficial start this week, with quarterbacks and rookies reporting to St. Joseph, Mo., on Friday.
With that in mind, here are five Chiefs who have something to prove over the next few weeks of practices.
The first one is obvious, and it will be the story of training camp.
Quarterback Patrick Mahomes has made remarkable strides since having surgery to repair a torn left ACL and LCL in December — he even participated during most of the team’s May and June practices. But there is still a lot he’ll have to prove physically before we know whether he’ll be available for Week 1.
Mahomes did non-contact work during summer drills (while wearing a heavy knee brace) but was held out of 11-on-11s as a precaution. He told reporters in late May that running and cutting would be the next milestones as he worked his way back.
One would expect the competitive Mahomes will want to get back to full work in training camp practices soon so he can test himself. So, how will he respond to having added stress on the knee? And what will it be like to work around some discomfort that’s likely to make him less mobile than in years past?
Mahomes will have a lot to prove to the medical staff — and himself — before he’s cleared to start the season opener.
Receiver Rashee Rice was my pick for the Chiefs player with the most on the line this season, and he enters 2026 at a career crossroads.
Entering the final year of his rookie contract, he has been unreliable over his three seasons, battling injuries while also making poor off-field choices that have too often dragged the Chiefs into negative headlines. The latest was when he violated his Dallas County probation and was forced to immediately serve a previously sentenced 30-day jail term this spring, which kept him away from the team during OTAs and mandatory minicamp.
Rice had cleanup surgery on his right knee in May that wasn’t expected to be serious, but it’s another thing to monitor in training camp as he looks to regain the confidence of coaches and teammates.
A wide range of outcomes is possible. If Rice is healthy and available, he could be in line for huge production in an offense that values and accentuates his run-after-catch ability.
With another injury or away-from-football slip-up, though? It’s tough to gauge exactly what Rice’s free-agency market might be if he goes through another lost season.
Training camp figures to be critical for Rice as he needs to show he’s healthy and quickly rebuild chemistry with Mahomes after missing those May and June reps.
One of the most significant things we learned during minicamp in June was this team is entering the season with an open competition at right tackle.
That’s probably a surprise if you weren’t following along until now. Veteran Jaylon Moore — the Chiefs signed him to a two-year free-agent deal in 2025 — was the presumed starter heading into summer practice, but coach Andy Reid acknowledged in June that the team was sorting through options with Esa Pole and Kahlil Benson also competing for the role.
The Chiefs often value competition to motivate guys, so maybe this offseason talk is just a ploy to fire up Moore and have him enter camp driven to win the job from the start.
It’s still at least a little concerning for a win-now team that it is considering a pair of young undrafted free agents in Pole (2025) and Benson (2026) for such a vital piece on the front line.
Kansas City tends not to mask things much during training camp practices with its rotations. We’ll definitely be watching to see who takes the first snap at right tackle next week — probably Moore — and then who sticks at that spot over the next few weeks.
This much is certain: Moore still has work to do if he wants to prove he’s the best guy for the job.
There are two truths when it comes to rookie cornerback Mansoor Delane:
1. Because the team traded up to select him with the No. 6 pick , he needs to be an immediate starter.
2. He didn’t get off to a smooth start in spring practices, sitting out mandatory minicamp with a shoulder injury.
The second note might seem minor, but it could quickly turn into a big deal if Delane shows any ill effects when he arrives this week. Defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo greatly values on-field reps for newcomers who are learning his complex scheme, and we can look to last season for a relevant data point.
Free-agent cornerback Kristian Fulton missed part of training camp after right knee cleanup surgery, with Spagnuolo later saying it took a while for Fulton to earn trust and get caught up with the playbook. After that, Fulton struggled to see the field until deep into the season, when he held his own as a starter in the final two games.
Reid, for his part, said in June he expected Delane to be ready to go for the start of camp. There’s also nothing wrong with early precaution, especially for a key player on the defense.
None of that changes the reality, though. Delane faces pressure to perform right away after the Chiefs made their biggest draft bet on him.
The depth chart — for most of the offseason — made it seem like the defense could use another rotational player at edge rusher.
That signing never came, which could lead one to believe the Chiefs have at least some hope that 2023 first-round pick Felix Anudike-Uzomah can be a contributor if he stays healthy.
There’s no way to describe Anudike-Uzomah’s tenure as anything but a disappointment. The Chiefs have had to constantly backfill at edge rusher after he didn’t develop as anticipated, though the Kansas State product also hasn’t had the best luck with health. His latest setback came last preseason, when he suffered a hamstring injury that resulted in a season-long injured reserve stint.
In the final year of his rookie contract, Anudike-Uzomah remains crazy young. He turned 24 in January, which means he actually was born about nine months after Chargers rookie edge rusher Akheem Mesidor, who was the 22nd pick in April’s draft.
From that aspect, it’s not too late for Anudike-Uzomah to flash some of the potential he displayed in college. Either way, he’ll be one to watch in training camp to see if anything has clicked this offseason.
His NFL future — with the Chiefs or otherwise — has a lot riding on these next few months.

title: Myles Garrett? Puka Nacua? Ranking 10 most essential Rams with camp set to open Trent McDuffie? Matthew Stafford? Davante Adams? A stacked roster with Super Bowl aspirations makes for an intriguing list. Nate Atkins
summary:

full_text:
Puka Nacua led the NFL with 129 receptions in 2025. Kevin Terrell / Getty Images
WOODLAND HILLS, Calif. — Training camp is just about here, and with it will come the start of a “Super Bowl or bust” season for the Los Angeles Rams.
They have one of the most loaded rosters in the NFL, an experienced and connected group fresh off a narrow loss in the NFC Championship Game. They’ve made the biggest splashes of any team this offseason, with two trades for All-Pro defenders. They have star power, but they also have more reliance on some of those stars than others.
Here, we’re ranking the top 10 most essential Rams to this season’s success. It’s a subjective list and a subjective process, but to get there, we’re asking two questions about each player on this year’s roster:
1. What does the team’s ceiling become if this player reaches his? 2. How much of a setback will it be if this player has to miss a month of games?
Value is a different conversation than best, of course. It factors in positional importance, depth at that position, value to specific schemes, proven ability, age and demonstrated upside.
This one will be up for debate because of the great players left off the list and the fact that Williams arguably has the best backup behind him of any of these options in Blake Corum, not to mention another intriguing option in Jarquez Hunter. He also doesn’t play a premium position.
But to understand the scheme Sean McVay and Matthew Stafford have built together, you have to appreciate what Williams brings perhaps better than any other player at his position in the sport. His ability to identify and stonewall blitzers in pass protection makes him essential to keeping his quarterback safe from the most vicious and hard-to-escape hits, and allows Stafford’s superpowers to come to life.
Add his consistency and durability with three straight seasons of at least 1,100 rushing yards, his steady receiving skills that have been a bit underutilized with the talent at wideout and his presence as one of the team’s biggest leaders, and it’s hard to envision the Rams’ offense operating the same way without him.
Here’s another player at a non-premium position cracking the top 10. But if you watched the Rams last season with and without Dotson, it shouldn’t come as a surprise.
On pure ability, Dotson is the best offensive lineman on the roster. I had an opposing defensive coach say he scared him far more than any of their other starters up front. That’s because Dotson is massive at 6-foot-4, 330 pounds, which lets him not only operate in good coordination in the Rams’ zone blocking schemes but also reach the second level and put linebackers and safeties in the dirt. Some of Los Angeles’ most explosive runs come when Dotson pulls this off. He’s a huge reason why Coleman Shelton and Warren McClendon Jr. have fit in nicely in that run scheme.
But what elevates him here is his ability to protect the pocket so nicely for a 38-year-old quarterback who doesn’t have the mobility to escape internal pressure. Dotson has allowed just nine sacks in six career seasons. Last year, teams generated a sack against Dotson on just 0.6 percent of pass rushing snaps, according to Sports Info Solutions.
Now, we are moving on to the positions that typically reserve the most value in this league. Given the state of Stafford’s back and age, both tackles are almost a must for a list like this, and McClendon has shown enough to be more than just a man filling a spot.
McClendon broke out last season after replacing Rob Havenstein. He started 13 games between the regular season and postseason and impressed in the run game, allowing it to get better and better by the week. His best value came in pass protection, where he played 383 snaps and gave up just two sacks.
It was an incredible find for a team that needed to protect Stafford at all costs, and it’s all the more valuable now with Havenstein retired and no one remotely proven to step in if McClendon goes down.
The players so far on this list have had something in common: protecting Stafford. Now comes one who is more about maximizing the veteran quarterback.
Adams arrived a year ago as a replacement for Cooper Kupp, and it wasn’t always a smooth transition. Consistent production and durability were both concerns, but the highs were impossible to ignore. Adams played 14 games and led the NFL with 14 receiving touchdowns. He and Stafford found a red zone cheat code around midseason, allowing Adams to score 11 times in the final eight games.
Adams finished with 789 yards, his fewest since 2015. He battled lingering lower-body injuries and is now 33. So the concerns exist, but that’s also why he’s incredibly important to keep on the field. The Rams struggled on third downs and in the red zone until they found this connection at midseason, and the attention on Puka Nacua will be too difficult to work through if Adams isn’t out there and the Rams are relying on what they have behind him, which is among the least proven depth on the roster.
If you asked anyone around the Rams defense early last season who the most valuable defender was, Lake’s name consistently came up. When he went down at midseason, his value became all the more clear.
As a versatile, tough, communicative defensive back, Lake embodies everything defensive coordinator Chris Shula wants from his dime-heavy scheme. As the captain of the secondary, Lake bounced from nickel cornerback to free safety to strong safety, making it difficult early on for opponents to diagnose his alignment and role. When he missed six games to an elbow dislocation, a secondary light on investments at outside cornerback saw immediate regression, and so did the run defense.
Lake’s late-season return didn’t quite spark a total turnaround. He was just one player for offenses to account for with easy options to throw to outside. This spring’s cornerback overhaul is partly about forcing quarterbacks to throw Lake’s way more, where the Rams believe he has far more potential than his one career interception demonstrates. (He did finish with 10 passes defensed in 10 games.)
After all, the Rams believed so much in him that they gave him a three-year, $38.3 million extension the moment he came back from injured reserve last season.
Here comes the first blockbuster addition of the offseason. Of the Rams’ three new added starters, none of them has the ability to offer the upgrade that McDuffie does, given his All-Pro ability at a premium position that killed the Rams down the stretch last season.
McDuffie will primarily play outside cornerback, which is what enabled him to sign a four-year deal for $31 million per season, the largest deal ever for a cornerback. But his versatility was just as intriguing to the Rams, as he can also bounce inside and offer even better play at nickel, given his instincts, communication and toughness at 5-foot-11, 193 pounds.
That’s Lake’s position to start, but McDuffie is what will allow Lake to move around. Those two are this high on the list for the ways they’ll maximize each other.
This top four forms its own tier. That’s why it can feel too low to have Nacua here, but that’s just how many stars the Rams have at the top of their roster.
Nacua was a 1B to Jaxon Smith-Njigba as the best receiver in the game last season. He led the NFL with 129 catches and 107.2 receiving yards per game. He plays the kind of high-volume, yards-after-contact style that McVay loves as the engine of his offense, and he managed to play 19 games despite all those vicious hits. He’s as consistent as sunrise and sunset —he’s averaged 95.3 receiving yards per game through his first three seasons, an all-time NFL mark.
Losing Nacua for any stretch of time would be brutal, as the Rams simply don’t have anyone who profiles anywhere near his volume or consistency in moving the chains and defeating zone coverages. If that happens, Los Angeles would have to lean on the run game and throwing to tight ends a bunch, which…

title: The Patriots' biggest remaining questions as training camp nears We already know a lot about the 2026 Patriots. But several big questions remain, including a potential extension for Gonzalez. Chad Graff
summary:
Pro Bowl cornerback Christian Gonzalez is eligible for an extension. Could one be on the horizon ahead of Week 1? Thearon W. Henderson / Getty Images
At long last, the New England Patriots’ offseason is just about over. The first practice of training camp is Saturday. The season opener in Seattle is less than seven weeks away.
At this point, we already know a lot about the Patriots. The big offseason moves are done. The coaching staff is in place.
Still, with the first practices on the horizon,
full_text:
Pro Bowl cornerback Christian Gonzalez is eligible for an extension. Could one be on the horizon ahead of Week 1? Thearon W. Henderson / Getty Images
At long last, the New England Patriots’ offseason is just about over. The first practice of training camp is Saturday. The season opener in Seattle is less than seven weeks away.
At this point, we already know a lot about the Patriots. The big offseason moves are done. The coaching staff is in place.
Still, with the first practices on the horizon, a few questions linger. Let’s look at the biggest remaining questions as training camp begins.
Gonzalez has been eligible to sign an extension for months, but a deal has not been reached. That apparently irked the cornerback enough that he barely participated in spring practices.
On one hand, these sorts of deals get done in August all the time. That would suggest there’s little cause for concern yet regarding the long-term future of one of the franchise’s best players.
On the other hand, if the Pats don’t get a deal done by Week 1, the story threatens to cloud Gonzalez’s season.
Still just 24 years old, Gonzalez has a legit argument to reset the cornerback market and become the league’s highest-paid player at the position.
The feeling around the NFL is that an extension will get done between the Patriots and Gonzalez. But after Gonzalez skipped optional practices this spring and was a limited participant in mandatory ones, his status bears monitoring as training camp begins.
The Patriots wanted to improve their rushing game this offseason, so they signed Julian Hill to a three-year, $15 million contract, which raised some critics’ eyebrows. But the term reflected the Patriots’ desire to solidify their No. 2 tight end spot with a strong blocker.
But Hill suffered a season-ending injury earlier this offseason. That puts the Patriots in a potentially difficult spot behind Hunter Henry at the position.
They drafted Eli Raridon in the third round but acknowledged he needed to get stronger to adapt to the NFL game. They had hoped he’d have most of this season to learn while serving as the No. 3 option behind Henry and Hill.
The Patriots are also expected to utilize multiple-tight-end formations at a high rate this season, so they need a good No. 2. In camp, it’ll be interesting to follow how quickly Raridon, 22, picks up a position that’s often difficult for rookies.
New England doesn’t have a lot of other options. CJ Dippre will open camp on the physically unable to perform list. Jack Westover and Tanner Arkin were the other options before they signed Mitch Van Vooren, an undrafted player in 2025, on Wednesday.
So if there’s a position where the Patriots look to pull off an August trade or nab someone off the waiver wire, it’ll probably be tight end.
A year ago, Boutte was arguably the Patriots’ best wide receiver and one of the NFL’s best deep threats. This season, he enters training camp with an undefined role after the team brought in A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs. Last year’s third-round pick, Kyle Williams, continues to develop.
That seems to have bothered Boutte, who skipped voluntary practices this spring, and it’s easy to understand his frustration. He has now played for three head coaches in three years and gotten better each season. Finally, he felt like he had carved out a role.
And now, as he enters a contract year, his role is being diminished. Because of that, he could try to force his way out. At the same time, though, the Patriots don’t have much motivation to move him.
It sets up a potentially trying situation. The best-case scenario for the Patriots is probably that Boutte comes to camp motivated and easily wins a competition for the No. 3 wide receiver job. Which brings us to …
After several seasons in flux, the Patriots have clearly defined roles at the top of the wide receiver depth chart. Brown will be one of the team’s outside wide receivers and the No. 1 target. Doubs will be the No. 2 option.
But it’s unclear who the No. 3 guy will be. Traditionally, that would be someone who could play in the slot. It’s a role that could be occupied by DeMario Douglas or Efton Chism, either of whom could earn time with a strong training camp.
But in a season in which the Patriots are expected to utilize a lot of heavy personnel groupings, the No. 3 wide receiver could still be an outside option who could spell Brown or Doubs, which opens the door for players like Boutte, Williams and Mack Hollins.
Further down the depth chart, it’ll also be interesting to see who makes the team. The Patriots can probably only keep six receivers, which could mean one of Boutte, Douglas, Chism or Hollins gets cut.
The New England defense played so well down the stretch last season that it was a no-brainer when the team named Zak Kuhr the full-time defensive coordinator.
But while Drake Maye was criticized for the team’s easy schedule a year ago, it actually helped the defense more than it did the offense. The Patriots played only two offenses (the Buffalo Bills and New York Giants) that ranked in the top 10 of expected points per play last season.
There are plenty of reasons to believe this year’s defense will be just as good, if not better. The unit improved at safety. The linebacker depth should be better.
But the defense still has plenty to prove entering an important season, and it’ll be interesting to see how it fares in training camp against an offense that should be really, really good.
Rookies reported to training camp this week, and Jacas remains unsigned after undergoing a medical procedure earlier this offseason. He didn’t attend spring practices, and now that he remains unsigned with camp set to begin, it’s fair to wonder whether Week 1 might be in jeopardy for the edge rusher from Illinois.
It’s clear by now that even when he signs, he’ll be behind the team’s other rookies. But if this lingers much longer, it’s fair to wonder whether Jacas will even be ready to play at the start of the season.
That would be a big blow for the Patriots since Jacas was supposed to be the rookie they leaned on most this season — and because fellow edge rusher Harold Landry is set to open training camp on the physically unable to perform list as his rehab continues.

title: Giants’ 10-step plan revisited: Will New York regret lack of investment in trenches? The Giants didn't hire John Harbaugh to oversee a rebuild, but did they do enough to help the coach turn them into NFC contenders? Dan Duggan 1

The New York Giants had more direction this offseason than in previous years. With the hiring of coach John Harbaugh and the promise of quarterback Jaxson Dart’s rookie season, it made sense for the Giants to be aggressive.

full_text:
The New York Giants added two young building blocks to their core during the NFL Draft with their first-round selections of Arvell Reese and Frances Mauigoa. Tom Horak / Imagn Images
The New York Giants had more direction this offseason than in previous years. With the hiring of coach John Harbaugh and the promise of quarterback Jaxson Dart’s rookie season, it made sense for the Giants to be aggressive.
The 63-year-old Harbaugh wasn’t hired to oversee a lengthy rebuild. And a quarterback’s rookie contract is a prime window for a team to spend on the rest of the roster. Of course, the Giants had to exercise some discipline with a roster that won seven games combined over the past two seasons.
So, with that in mind, I penned my annual offseason plan in February. With training camp set to kick off July 29, here’s a review of how my 10-step plan compares to the Giants’ actions:
The Giants made the obvious decision to cut Okereke for $9 million in cap savings. I planned to direct those savings into a replacement, proposing Leo Chenal, who signed a three-year, $24.75 million contract with the Washington Commanders in free agency.
The Giants signed Tremaine Edmunds, who hadn’t been released by the Chicago Bears when my plan was published, to a three-year, $36 million contract. Edmunds is a proven every-down Mike linebacker who should seamlessly step into Okereke’s role.
The Giants also cut offensive lineman James Hudson and kicker Graham Gano to create $9.9 million in cap savings. Instead of cutting running back Devin Singletary for $5.25 million in cap savings, the Giants negotiated a pay cut to the minimum salary to save $4 million and keep the experienced backup.
As expected, the Giants had to restructure the contracts of left tackle Andrew Thomas and outside linebacker Brian Burns to create cap space. Those moves freed up $26.1 million in cap space this year.
The Giants traded defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence, which produced $13 million in cap savings. Cornerback Paulson Adebo remains the player with the most potential cap savings from a restructure, but the Giants have enough room that they may be able to avoid that move.
I knew Lawrence wouldn’t be content to play out the final two years of a contract that dropped below market value as it progressed. So I proposed a proactive extension, landing on $28 million per year as a fair compromise. That’s exactly what Lawrence got, but it was a bumpy road to that resolution.
I knew the situation had the potential to go south, but I didn’t grasp how toxic it would become. As the relationship reached the point of no return, the Giants got a lifeline from the desperate Cincinnati Bengals, who offered the No. 10 pick for Lawrence. Such a strong return made it palatable to part with a player who isn’t far removed from being viewed as the best interior defensive lineman in the NFL.
I was willing to bet on Lawrence returning to dominant form (he was still ranked the No. 7 interior defensive lineman in the league, off a down season, in an ESPN poll of league evaluators) once he was satisfied with his compensation. It seems like a lock for that to happen with a fresh start in Cincinnati.
Even if Lawrence returns to being an unblockable game-wrecker, the Giants can take solace that they acquired a potential building block in offensive lineman Francis Mauigoa with the 10th pick. That makes Lawrence’s exit much different from other high-profile departures in recent years.
A durable blocker whose best NFL role may be as a guard rather than right tackle.
The Giants shared my approach on Thibodeaux by listening to trade proposals. I was willing to move Thibodeaux for a Day 2 draft pick. That was the sweet spot for the Giants, although their asking price jumped to the second round after Thibodeaux made a strong first impression on Harbaugh.
The Giants were never getting a second-rounder; the best offer was a fourth-round pick from the New Orleans Saints. I understand the decision to resist that meager return.
The Giants are trying to win with Harbaugh and Dart, so giving away a quality player for a Day 3 pick doesn’t fit that mindset. The edge depth that is the team’s strength would immediately become a weakness if they traded Thibodeaux and Burns or Abdul Carter got hurt.
Thibodeaux’s future is unclear, but the Giants have options. They still could deal him at the trade deadline, or they could factor his free-agent departure next offseason into the comp pick formula. There’s an outside chance they could re-sign him if he has a great season in his new role.
Re-signing Eluemunor was my top priority in free agency. There was a wide range of projected contracts throughout the offseason, but Eluemunor’s three-year, $39 million contract wound up close to the three-year, $36 million projection by Pro Football Focus used in my plan. That’s an extremely reasonable price tag to ensure stability at a critical spot.
Flott was a tougher call. I was in favor of keeping him because he’s only 24, and last season might have been the start of his prime. It was challenging to nail down a contract projection for Flott, but I was comfortable going up to $12 million annually. The Giants likely shared that valuation as they tried to re-sign Flott but declined to match the three-year, $45 million deal he received from the Tennessee Titans.
That’s a healthy contract for a player with one season of high-level performance, but a case can be made to overextend for homegrown players who blossom during their rookie contracts. Flott’s cap hit this year is $10.7 million compared to $8 million for replacement Greg Newsome, who signed a one-year prove-it deal after consecutive subpar seasons.
Flott’s cap hits increase in the future, but the Giants could be paying a No. 2 cornerback then. The hope is that second-round pick Colton Hood provides quality production at a discount price.
I expected Robinson to have the highest price tag of the Giants’ top three internal free agents, and I was comfortable letting him walk for the type of bloated contract (four years, $70 million) he got from the Titans.
I proposed signing a mid-tier free agent like Kendrick Bourne, who got a two-year, $10 million contract from the Arizona Cardinals, to help offset Robinson’s departure.
Darnell Mooney, who wasn’t available when I made my plan, fits the bill and was even cheaper at $3 million for one year. I also recommended using a mid-round pick on a wide receiver, which the Giants did by trading up in the third round to select Notre Dame product Malachi Fields.
The 6-foot-4, 222-pound Fields has a different skill set than Robinson, but wide receivers come in all shapes and sizes, and the hope is Fields approaches Robinson’s production during his rookie contract.
Shades of Michael Pittman, but must work on expanding his route tree.
The trenches were the emphasis of my plan, with the intention of adding Franklin-Myers alongside Lawrence. There’s excitement about the Giants’ front-seven now, but imagine a front of Lawrence, Franklin-Myers, the trio of edge rushers and No. 5 pick Arvell Reese.
I prioritized Franklin-Myers over an investment in a linebacker like Edmunds. PFF projected a three-year, $45 million contract for Franklin-Myers, who blew that away with a three-year, $63 million deal from the Titans. I would have bowed out of the bidding at that point, and directing those funds toward a higher-caliber middle linebacker was an understandable pivot.
Seumalo has been on my radar each time he has hit the market in the past three years. He signed a three-year, $24 million contract with the Pittsburgh Steelers in 2023 and delivered three consistently strong seasons in Pittsburgh.
Seumalo, 32, signed a reasonable three-year, $31.5 million contract with the Cardinals this offseason. The Giants flirted with Alijah Vera-Tucker, but bowed out when he got a three-year, $42 million contract from the New England Patriots. I would have pounced on Seumalo at his price, especially at the…

title: Eagles' Cooper DeJean mastered slot corner. Can he do the same at safety? DeJean is an established difference-maker in the slot. But playing part time at safety could give the Eagles new options. Zach Berman
summary:
Philadelphia Eagles CB Cooper DeJean warms up before a game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Lincoln Financial Field in 2024. Emilee Chinn / Getty Images
PHILADELPHIA — Cooper DeJean and Reed Blankenship hosted Vic Fangio on their podcast this summer. The visit brought an admission from the Philadelphia Eagles defensive coordinator about DeJean that Fangio first revealed in the spring and showcased during offseason practices, when DeJean played safety while the Eagles aligned in their base def
full_text:
Philadelphia Eagles CB Cooper DeJean warms up before a game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Lincoln Financial Field in 2024. Emilee Chinn / Getty Images
PHILADELPHIA — Cooper DeJean and Reed Blankenship hosted Vic Fangio on their podcast this summer. The visit brought an admission from the Philadelphia Eagles defensive coordinator about DeJean that Fangio first revealed in the spring and showcased during offseason practices, when DeJean played safety while the Eagles aligned in their base defense.
Fangio’s comment seemed especially relevant given that the star slot cornerback and the former starting safety shared the screen like they used to share the secondary.
“Your days at corner hopefully are over,” Fangio told him on “ Exciting Mics .” “… Coop is replacing Reed part time.”
The context to the statement is that DeJean, a first-team All-Pro in his second season, is an every-down player for the Eagles. On most snaps, that means he plays in the slot — where he was considered the best in the NFL. When the Eagles are not playing with five or six defensive backs in the formation, they still want DeJean on the field. The question becomes where he plays.
Last summer, DeJean alternated between cornerback and safety in the base defense, while Fangio tried to determine his best quartet. It was settled that DeJean would play at cornerback, where he lined up for about 22 percent of the defensive snaps last season. After the addition of Riq Woolen solidified the Eagles’ outside cornerback tandem with Quinyon Mitchell, DeJean will now focus on safety for any formation with four defensive backs.
“I’m excited,” DeJean said in the spring. “I did it a little bit last year during training camp. I’ve been around it and feel like I’ve gotten to learn all the roles in this defense pretty well. So, yeah, I’m excited. It’s a good challenge for me,  just trying to perfect that position now rather than going back and forth from safety to corner to nickel last year, just kind of sticking to that safety and nickel spot now. That’s been fun.”
DeJean’s been touted for his versatility since the Eagles drafted him in the 2024 draft’s second round out of Iowa and there were questions about which position he would play. (In Dane Brugler’s scouting report in “The Beast” in 2024, he wrote that DeJean offers an “NFL starter-quality skill set that fits interchangeably at cornerback, safety or nickel.”) Fangio said last summer that DeJean could be a “good safety.” DeJean defended a route in practice that had previously caused the Eagles’ defense problems. DeJean defended it “like he’d been a safety his whole life.”
DeJean said this spring that he’s been preparing for all three positions since he arrived. The close relationship with Blankenship, who was a three-year starter for the Eagles, rubbed off on DeJean. He also learned from C.J. Gardner-Johnson and Marcus Epps. He even peppered starting safety Drew Mukuba with questions when Mukuba was a rookie.
“Playing nickel in this defense is kind of like playing safety in a lot of ways,” DeJean said. “The techniques are pretty similar.”
This is often referenced with safety and nickel, which is why players can shift between those spots. Michael Carter II, a candidate to start at safety for the Eagles, has been a slot cornerback throughout his NFL career. A cornerback knows he has the sideline on one side of him. He’s often on an island, but those who play in the slot and those who play safety need to mind all directions, while also navigating traffic in the middle of the field.
But they’re not the same positions, carrying different responsibilities and different spacing on the field.
“Anytime you move a little bit further away from the ball, now you’re talking about enhancing your vision and being able to maximize your visual tools, right?” said Eagles defensive backs coach Joe Kasper, who had previously been the team’s safeties coach. “The trick at safety is now things happen a little bit slower. I’m a little bit further away, but I’ve got to determine angles and space and time and distance a little bit differently. So, we’ve got to get him used to that.
“Everything that he’s done at nickel, though, indicates that the understanding and feel for time and distance is not a bridge too far for him. That’s where maybe you’d see guys struggle with going from one spot to the other. He doesn’t have those issues that we actually enhance that element within how he plays the nickel position. So to me, it’s another way for us to continue to maximize a resource that we have.”
DeJean is already one of the top young players in football, if only judged by the difference-maker he is at slot cornerback. He’s productive in coverage and against the run. He’s a physical player with size and athleticism. DeJean totaled 85 tackles last season with 16 passes defended, four tackles for losses and two interceptions.
And his youth should not be understated. DeJean turned 23 in February. He’s younger than multiple defensive backs drafted this spring, including second-round picks Treydan Stukes and Bud Clark. Kasper said the “sky is the limit for him.”
“He’s special in a lot of ways,” Kasper said in May. “The mental approach is outstanding, physical tools are outstanding, how he interacts with teammates is outstanding, how he interacts with me and the other coaches is outstanding. There’s not really a false note to him. It’s on me, and then on him too, to continue to grow and build. … He’s on a nice track, but there’s things he’s got to work on and get better at, too.
“We’ve got a long time, obviously, between now and when we’ll see the final product for this year. So, we got to continue to chip things off, check things off of his list, but his versatility is a huge asset for us, and that’s about his mindset and his approach, both technical understanding, schematic understanding, but also just how he approaches his day-to-day.”
During the offseason, DeJean studied Pro Football Hall of Famer Charles Woodson — one of the most versatile defensive backs in NFL history. Woodson was an All-Pro at cornerback and safety. He spent time in the slot before it carried some of its present-day luster. But DeJean said the best way for him to learn is to play in the defense, and this summer offers him a better chance to find comfort in the role than last summer when the Eagles tried finding the best combination. The Eagles report to training camp on July 28.
DeJean at safety also offers the Eagles flexibility with how to approach the defense. Fangio’s unit is set to be one of the NFL’s best. There are few question marks in the group. One is at safety, where the Eagles lost Blankenship in free agency to the Houston Texans and did not make a high-profile addition to replace him. Veteran Marcus Epps returns and is the favorite to start next to Mukuba, whose rookie season ended with an injury. Carter will spend time at safety.
The Eagles traded away Sydney Brown , a former third-round pick who did not find his rhythm in Fangio’s defense. Fangio termed the second safety spot when the Eagles are in nickel as an “open competition.” And when he was first asked about the position, he revealed DeJean would play there in base.
What remains unknown is how much weight DeJean adding safety to his repertoire storyline should carry. Fangio’s history would not suggest base defense will be heavily featured. The Eagles have played more snaps in nickel than any team in the NFL during Fangio’s two seasons and ranked No. 3 last season. DeJean is an established difference-maker in the slot. But playing DeJean deep at safety could also give the Eagles options. Mukuba, who spent time as a slot defender in college, offers the Eagles four starting defensive backs who can cover in base. Add in the athleticism of linebackers Zack Baun and Jihaad Campbell, who both have range in coverage, and the Eagles could have flexibility to play more five-man fronts if they choose because of the way they can cover in the…

title: Jacoby Brissett Present as Cardinals Begin Training Camp
full_text:
ARIZONA — If you're reading this, the Arizona Cardinals have reported for training camp.
2026 is unofficially underway with first-year Mike LaFleur leading the charge, though his projected starting quarterback does not have a new deal.
The Cardinals and Jacoby Brissett haven't found middle ground on a new contract that would give the veteran passer more guaranteed money on the final year of his contract.
Brissett, however, is present per reports.
#AZCardinals QB Jacoby Brissett reported to training camp today along with the rest of his teammates, sources tell me and @RapSheet . Nothing new as of right now on his contract but Brissett is in the building. pic.twitter.com/UD1zam3KNl
There was hope after rookie passer Carson Beck struck a deal , Brissett would be next, and Arizona could move into the future with no more unnecessary headlines surrounding the position.
That's yet to come to fruition, and as Arizona gears up for their first practice of camp, Brissett is likely to be a bystander if no deal is met according to NFL insider Ian Rapoport.
"Jacoby Brissett, no news yet on a possible new deal. I would expect him to show up and kind of just stand around until he gets a deal. But the team does want to give him a raise. They believe he's worthy of it and deserves it, so the hope is they will come together and figure something out."
"There's no news yet on a possible new deal for Jacoby Brissett.. The team does wanna give him a raise and the hope is that they can figure something out" @RapSheet #PMSLive pic.twitter.com/9AhXCrdlwB
Brissett is likely to be a hold-in if there's no new contract agreed upon by Arizona's first practice, which should save him some money. Players who are not in attendance for training camp are fined $60,000 per day with no possibility for those fines to be waived.
The exact number Brissett is hoping to reach remains unknown, though it is odd the Cardinals have reportedly been willing to work with him on getting a reworked deal.
Budda Baker seems to believe Brissett is asking for below the bare minimum.
Just want bro to get his shit done… he is not asking for what you think. Bro is asking for below the bare minimum. Let’s just get it done!!!
LaFleur has been supportive of Brissett's prior absence during offseason team activities and non-participation during mandatory minicamp, though it will be interesting to see where he stands if Brissett is again on the sidelines as training camp practices begin on Thursday.
Brissett has a strong rapport with Arizona's top weapons in Trey McBride and Marvin Harrison Jr. entering 2026, and combined with his veteran experience, he's the obvious choice to start for the Cardinals in Week 1.
Yet there appears to be a hold-up on Arizona's end, as many believe Brissett eventually will be replaced under center if the Cardinals are again at the bottom of the league standings halfway through the season.
One side will ultimately blink before negotiations are done. We'll see who it is.

title: Cardinals Roster Tiers, Part 7: Franchise Cornerstones
full_text:
Welcome to the final installment of our series ranking every player on the Arizona Cardinals' roster ahead of training camp. This is part seven of our tiered saga, and if you missed any of the prior six, you can click on the respective links below:
We arrive at the very top tier of Arizona's roster: franchise cornerstones. These guys are the building blocks of the future for the Cardinals.
As a reminder, players are not ranked within the actual tier itself.
Players in this tier: Trey McBride, Paris Johnson Jr., Walter Nolen III, Jeremiyah Love
We'll start first with McBride, who is very arguably the best tight end in football and is riding high off one of the league's best statistical seasons at the position in quite some time, if not ever. McBride is a dominant force at the position, and fresh off a historical contract extension, he followed with historical production.
That should continue in 2026 with new head coach Mike LaFleur at the helm, who should be able to scheme McBride open better than ever. Yet McBride is so undeniably good he will produce under any circumstance. McBride, much like Thanos in the Avengers movie series, is inevitable.
Johnson is perhaps the most controversial name here, though the former No. 6 pick is the undisputed anchor for Arizona's offensive line. Johnson arguably could have been a Pro Bowl selection in either of the last two seasons if not for injuries.
Johnson's due for a contract extension and should receive a nice payday, although it won't reset the market. He's not quite in the elite territory, though Johnson is a very strong presence at left tackle and is emerging into a leader in the locker room. He deserves to be in this tier until proven otherwise.
Nolen is an exciting talent, and if he is able to stay healthy, he has the makings to become one of the best from his draft class. His elite athleticism and pass rush ability makes him a young game-wrecker in the trenches, something the Cardinals haven't had in quite some time.
It's on Nolen to hold up his end of the bargain and stay healthy, which hopefully should be the case after injuries derailed his rookie season. However, Nolen is so obviously a star in the making. He has everything to be a force in this league for years to come.
Finally, Love was one of the most polarizing draft picks in quite some — and that conversation will continue until he can prove his third overall pick price tag worthy. Love's place as a running back drafted high will leave no gray area in expectations for his career.
The good news? Love emerged from Notre Dame as one of college football's top playmakers, possessing the ability to change the dynamic of a game on any given touch in either the pass or ground game.
If he can translate that to the NFL, the Cardinals could have a special offense — spearheaded by a special talent in the backfield.

title: Cardinals Officially Lose Exciting Rookie to Injured Reserve
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals made a handful of roster moves today, one being an unfortunate placement of rookie defensive lineman Kaleb Proctor on injured reserve.
Proctor suffered a torn meniscus during the offseason, as confirmed by head coach Mike LaFleur — who believes it will be a significant injury.
"Kaleb Proctor had a meniscus tear, so he'll miss quite a bit of time. If not — I don't want to say absolute — but if not the whole year," he told reporters last month.
Arizona signed defensive lineman Coziah Izzard to fill his spot ahead of training camp.
Proctor, a fourth-round pick from Southeastern Louisiana, was the first FCS player taken in the 2026 draft. He is an elite athlete in the defensive interior but was considered undersized for the position.
“I use my arm length. I think I have 33-inch arms. I use my length and my quickness and my speed to beat the offensive guards and tackles," Proctor said after being drafted with the 104th pick.
"I feel like I bring a twitchiness to the table. An explosiveness. I’m quick out of my stance and (I have) a quick first step.”
Proctor and Walter Nolen III were projected to be a dynamic duo in Arizona's defensive interior this season, as both have the capability of emerging as disruptors up front. However, the potential of that tandem may have to wait.
Proctor's just the latest Cardinals rookie defensive lineman to suffer an injury before their debut, following in the footsteps of Nolen and Darius Robinson — both of whom suffered calf injuries ahead of their first season.
“I watched (DL) Walter Nolen (III). He’s just a freak of an athlete. dominant in the run, dominant in the pass—very hybrid. The D-line is just stacked," Proctor added after being drafted.
"The guy that announced the pick (DL Roy Lopez) that was awesome. But, getting up there (on my visit) with (guys like) (OL) Paris Johnson (Jr.) and seeing those guys and seeing all of the work that they put in. I got to see those guys kind of work out, so it was awesome.”
More from the Cardinals' press release on Izzard:
"Izzard (6-3, 305) spent his rookie season in 2025 on the practice squads of the Saints and Chiefs after entering the league with Kansas City as an undrafted free agent from Penn State. In five seasons at Penn State, Izzard played 51 games and had 78 tackles (40 solo), 17.5 tackles for loss, 9.0 sacks, and two forced fumbles. Izzard will wear jersey #93."

title: Cardinals Finally Get Carson Beck Contract Done
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals finally have Carson Beck under contract.
Beck, who was Arizona's final rookie to sign from the 2026 draft class, reportedly put pen to paper to get a deal done as the Cardinals report to training camp today.
From NFL insider Ian Rapoport on X:
"The #AZCardinals and rookie QB Carson Beck have agreed to terms and he will sign his four-year, $7.4M contract, sources say. One of the last picks to sign."
The #AZCardinals and rookie QB Carson Beck have agreed to terms and he will sign his four-year, $7.4M contract, sources say. One of the last picks to sign. pic.twitter.com/47C64qDe8T
Beck was waiting alongside Fernando Mendoza, Ty Simpson and Drew Allar as top quarterbacks taken this past April to sign their rookie deal.
Why did it take so long for Beck to sign? As a third-round pick, Beck was likely in search of getting his deal mostly (if not fully) guaranteed. Only first-round picks have their deals guaranteed in terms of money.
The NFL uses rookie scale contracts for draft picks, so there's not a whole lot of wiggle room for contract negotiations. However, guarantees, bonus structures and offsetting languages are often the biggest roadblocks for rookies.
Beck, having led Georgia and Miami to respective college football national championship appearances, has the prototypical size (6-4) and game manager ability to step in and orchestrate an NFL offense during his rookie season, which made him an attractive pick when the Cardinals were on the clock.
Beck will compete with Jacoby Brissett , Gardner Minshew and Kedon Slovis in Arizona's quarterback room during training camp. The Cardinals have their first training camp practice on Thursday.
Beck enters 2026 in perhaps one of the most unique circumstances in his draft class. The Cardinals very much are contenders to take a quarterback in 2027, though Arizona will first need to see what they have in Beck before pulling the trigger.
The problem ? Beck is buried on the depth chart and will likely not have ample sample size as a starter.
"There is a lot of things to learn, but the more time that I spend and the more reps you get, the more comfortable you get with it and the more it just kind of feels like you're looking at the back of your hand," Beck said on learning an NFL playbook.
Beck was considered to be one of the more pro-ready passers in this class, and with Brissett not expected to last the entire season — it feels more like when, not if, we will see Beck under center for Arizona.

title: The Number That Could Finally End Cardinals, Jacoby Brissett Contract Battle
full_text:
ARIZONA — We're nearing the final hours before the Arizona Cardinals report to training camp on Wednesday, July 22 — and Jacoby Brissett's contract situation still isn't resolved.
It's been a storyline that's hung over the organization since the early beginnings of the offseason. After parting with Kyler Murray and whiffing on Malik Willis, the Cardinals deemed Brissett their starter for 2026.
Brissett, on the final year of his deal, wants more than the $1.5 million guaranteed on his contract. The Cardinals reportedly have been in agreement that a raise is due, though the two sides were far apart on what that number consists of.
"A day before the Cardinals report, and there is not yet a resolution to Jacoby Brissett’s contract situation," Ian Rapoport posted on X. "AZ and Brissett (who is his own agent) have been actively negotiating for the last several months and agree he’s due a raise. No consensus yet on the number."
Cardinals teammates have been vocal in their support of Brissett, the most recent coming from longtime team captain Budda Baker on social media:
Just want bro to get his shit done… he is not asking for what you think. Bro is asking for below the bare minimum. Let’s just get it done!!!
Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur has backed Brissett at every opportunity when asked about the veteran quarterback, who hasn't participated in any OTA or minicamp practice but was spotted getting off-field work in recently with offensive stars in Trey McBride and Marvin Harrison Jr.
Arizona likely doesn't want to roll out rookie Carson Beck immediately while Gardner Minshew isn't exactly a top option, either. Brissett has an established rapport with the offense thanks to his 12 starts last season, a year where he went 1-11 as the team's starter despite putting up career-bests in passing yards and touchdowns.
The hang-up here is guaranteed money. Brissett doesn't want to be dubbed a starting quarterback and not be adequately paid like one, especially on the back half of a two-year deal that was essentially just supposed to be a backup quarterback contract.
In terms of total cash, Minshew is set to make just over $300,000 more than Brissett in 2026 (via Spotrac) . Minshew is set to have a guaranteed total of $5.14 million, far above Brissett's $1.5 million figure that does not include bonuses.
It does not seem as if Brissett wants more years added on to a deal: He wants more upfront dough guaranteed in the event that something happens. He's 33 and this could be his last opportunity to be a starting quarterback at the NFL level.
When looking at average quarterback guaranteed money per year entering the 2026 season, roughly $13 million is the estimate with names such as Baker Mayfield, Patrick Mahomes and Sam Darnold hovering around that line (per OverTheCap ).
Brissett's unique predicament makes this a tough projection. He's not close to any of the three quarterbacks in terms of talent nor is he on a multi-year deal or part of a franchise's future plans.
Brissett very likely is eying at least $10 million in guarantees, which would tie him for the lowest non-rookie amount alongside Kirk Cousins (h/t Josh Weinfuss, ESPN ).
That appears to be the golden number. Arizona, who likely will turn to another quarterback at some point in the 2026 season, probably isn't keen to make that happen.
And alas, the ongoing game of chicken continues to the final moments before the Cardinals report at State Farm Stadium.
Will Brissett settle for anything less than $10 million guaranteed? That's the new question, one that could be resolved in a matter of either hours or weeks.

title: Cardinals Roster Tiers, Part 6: The Difference-Makers
full_text:
Welcome to the second tier of our Arizona Cardinals roster rankings ahead of training camp. If you've missed any of the previous tiers, you can click on them below:
We've reached the second-to-last tier of the pyramid. It's been a fun ride, though only a total of seven players exist in the top two groups. Today we'll evaluate Arizona's trio of veteran difference-makers.
Three staples. Three defensive players. Three leaders in terms of their position group and overall level of play.
As a reminder, the players are not ranked within the tier itself.
Players in this tier : Budda Baker, Josh Sweat, Mack Wilson Sr.
Baker has been the engine of Arizona's defense for years now, making the Pro Bowl in all but one of his nine years in the NFL. He doesn't post flashy interception numbers but is a productive tackler and has free rein within Nick Rallis' defense to attack when/wherever — which is a privilege afforded to few.
That helps keep opposing offensive coordinators guessing, and Baker's role as a leader through another coaching staff change can't be overstated. He's still viewed as one of the top safeties in the league and will be the heart and soul of the Cardinals until he decides otherwise.
Sweat's sack production (12.5) in his first season with Arizona was second to none and probably deserved Pro Bowl recognition. Sweat is far and away the top (and only) pass rush threat in Arizona's outside linebacker room, and the Cardinals' willingness to leave his room untouched only heightens Sweat's importance to the team.
Without Jonathan Gannon in the desert, it will be interesting to see how Sweat builds on one of his best years in the league. However, no defense can thrive without a pass rush, and Sweat's the undisputed top person to reach the quarterback in Arizona.
Wilson isn't quite on the same star-name level as Baker or Sweat, though if you ever needed to evaluate his importance to Arizona's defense — you can take a look at last season. The Cardinals were night and day different after Wilson went down with a season-ending rib injury. The front seven looked like a shell of itself.
Wilson's a versatile athlete at inside linebacker that handles captain and green dot duties for the Cardinals. He's effective against the run, rushing the passer and dropping into coverage, too. There's not much Wilson can't do, and while he's not a Pro Bowl player (yet), he sure plays like it.
Wilson wears many hats for the Cardinals in terms of responsibility, and when healthy, he's a glue guy for Arizona's defense.

title: Cardinals Have 2 QB Contract Standoffs; They Both Want the Same Thing
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals report to training camp tomorrow (July 22) with two massive contracts still unresolved at the quarterback position.
Jacoby Brissett and Carson Beck are running out of time to arrive to State Farm Stadium with their desired deals in place. As of now, Gardner Minshew and Kedon Slovis are the only other quarterbacks on the roster.
Brissett is under contract through the end of 2026, though he's been holding out for much of the offseason in hopes of getting more guaranteed money on a reworked deal.
NFL insider Ian Rapoport says the two sides are still at a stalemate.
"The Arizona Cardinals do not have their starting quarterback under a contract he would want to play under," Rapoport said.
From The Insiders on @NFLNetwork : A look at a few key pre-training camp storylines, focusing on the #AZCardinals and the #Vikings . pic.twitter.com/umbyWxFeEj
Brissett's current contains just shy of $2 million in guarantees, which is well below the number for starting quarterbacks across the league. The problem? Arizona reportedly told Brissett this offseason he would be the starter, which set the precedent for contract talks.
Brissett, when a reworked deal is in place, is expected to begin the season for Arizona as their starter — though the likelihood he finishes as their starter is low with Beck in the picture.
Beck, the Cardinals' third-round pick, is also looking to squeeze guaranteed money out of the Cardinals. NFL draft picks outside of the first round don't have their deals fully guaranteed, though Beck plays a premium position and is hoping to set a precedent for the future.
The NFL uses a rookie scale system for their contracts, so language and amount of guaranteed money within the deal are practically the only roadblocks to getting a deal done.
Beck isn't alone in his fight, however. All four quarterbacks taken in the first two days of the NFL Draft in Fernando Mendoza, Ty Simpson, Drew Allar and Beck have yet to put pen to paper.
The six remaining 2026 drafted rookies not yet under contract: • All 4 QBs taken in the first two days (Mendoza, Simpson, Beck, Allar) • Jermod McCoy, who was projected to be drafted much higher before injury concerns emerged • Gabe Jacas https://t.co/Cpjt5xFuqe
Beck is more than likely to show up to Day 1 festivities without a new deal than Brissett, though it is intriguing to see exactly who will budge first between organization and player on both fronts.
Brissett, 33 years old, is surely playing his final year in Arizona while Beck could potentially be an option for their future franchise quarterback spot.
There's varying levels of urgency for the Cardinals to strike deals with both before festivities begin. While Arizona reports on July 22, their first actual practice of 2026's training camp session won't be until July 23.

title: Marvin Harrison Jr. Sends Message Ahead of Cardinals' 2026 Season
full_text:
ARIZONA — Arizona Cardinals WR Marvin Harrison Jr. hears you loud and clear.
The third-year wideout enters 2026 with massive expectations following an up-and-down two seasons in Arizona. The Cardinals' first-round pick in 2024 (No. 4 overall) has failed to deliver on the generational label that followed him from Ohio State — though this year could be different.
There's a few reasons for that. Harrison has battled injuries and had to fight through a less-than-ideal role with prior offensive coordinator Drew Petzing, though 2026 is a clean slate with Mike LaFleur entering the picture.
Yet there's also been a few mishaps on Harrison's end, which has led to frustration on the fanbase's end.
Harrison posted the following message on his Instagram page:
"Knew I needed love but I think I value the hate more.."
Harrison, very loudly and clearly, has heard the flack he's received entering his third season — which is a massive one. After 2026 concludes, Arizona will have to make a decision on Harrison's fifth-year option as part of his rookie contract, which could track north of $20 million for the final year of his deal based off projections.
There's some that believe 2026 is a make-it-or-break-it season for Harrison, though there's no tougher critic on the wideout than the man himself.
"Personally, I just never really look at any positives. You probably should for your health but I don't really look at many positives, I always find the negatives," Harrison said when reflecting back on a tough 2025 season.
Harrison dealt with two heel injuries, a concussion and appendicitis in 2025. He missed five games.
"The injuries kind of sucked, honestly. The appendix really was the most importantly just like unfortunate [injury] because nothing I could really do about that,"  he said.
"Kind of just wrong timing and yeah, looking back on it just just sucks in general, because like I said, nothing I could do about it, but you just continue to move forward, continue to get better, really just kind of whole offseason that's really just thought about how unfortunate that situation was for me."
Harrison still projects to have a strong role in Arizona's attack moving into next season with names such as Trey McBride, Jeremiyah Love, Michael Wilson and others lingering as playmakers as well.
Harrison's potential still is through the roof — and he seems intent on realizing it this coming season.
